interview_metadata.name: Zoila Pizano
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised in El Paso, on the east side, and my whole life has felt very border-city, like English and Spanish always mixed together. My parents are from Mexican families, and at home we spoke Spanish a lot, especially with my grandma. My childhood was pretty family-centered: Sunday food, cousins coming over, Día de los Muertos altars, school projects on the kitchen table, and a lot of driving around between errands and family houses. I was always the kid drawing on notebook margins. In elementary school I liked making posters more than writing the actual report. In high school I got more serious about art because I had a teacher who let me try Adobe Illustrator and Photoshop, and that changed things for me. I started doing little flyers for clubs, painting backdrops, and helping with a community mural near a library program. I graduated high school, but I am not working a regular job right now. I have been helping at home, volunteering with youth art programs at the El Paso public library, and building a portfolio because I want to enroll in community college for graphic design or visual communication. I am not married, no kids, and I still live with my parents and younger brother. The big life events for me have been graduating, deciding not to rush into any random job, and trying to take art seriously even though money is tight and it feels risky.

follow_ups.question: What are some early memories that still shape how you think about yourself?
follow_ups.response: Making papel picado with my mom and grandma is one. Also my dad taking us to see murals around town, even if he did not call it art, just saying, 'Mira, they painted history right there.'

follow_ups.question: Who encouraged your art the most?
follow_ups.response: My high school art teacher, Ms. Rangel, and my mom. My mom would complain about the mess sometimes, but she saved my drawings in a folder.

follow_ups.question: What does a good future version of your life look like?
follow_ups.response: I want to be studying art, maybe working part time in a museum or nonprofit, and still doing murals that make Mexican-American families feel seen.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was after graduation. A few relatives were telling me to just get a full-time retail job right away, because that is practical and helps the house. Part of me understood that, but another part of me knew if I stopped making art completely, I would get stuck and lose confidence. Around that same time, the library youth art program needed volunteers for a pop-up exhibition, and I helped organize student pieces and design the little labels. Seeing younger kids get excited made me think, okay, this can be real work, not just a hobby. I decided to take a gap year, help at home, volunteer, and prepare for El Paso Community College instead of jumping into whatever job first. It was not a dramatic movie moment, but it mattered.

follow_ups.question: Who was on each side of that decision?
follow_ups.response: My dad leaned practical, like income first. My mom was more in the middle. My art teacher and my friend Alina were like, 'Do the portfolio, apply, do not wait too long.'

follow_ups.question: What did you actually do the week after deciding?
follow_ups.response: I made a list in my journal: portfolio pieces, FAFSA questions, EPCC deadlines, library volunteer days. Then I procrastinated for two days and finally organized my Illustrator files.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice, but messy. I did not wake up with one perfect plan; I had to keep choosing it every time someone asked, 'So what are you doing now?'

follow_ups.question: What made you stick with it?
follow_ups.response: Having actual deadlines helped. Also posting small art updates made me feel accountable.

follow_ups.question: Did you doubt it?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially when friends started earning money and I was still at home making portfolio revisions.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. I think more clear advising for first-generation students would have helped, especially about financial aid and art careers. Sometimes the information exists, but you do not know who to ask.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have been most useful?
follow_ups.response: A checklist, someone bilingual who could explain costs to my parents, and portfolio feedback.

follow_ups.question: Did any organization help at all?
follow_ups.response: The library and my high school art room helped emotionally, more than financially.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner and I do not have children. My family is my parents, Maribel and Rogelio, my younger brother Mateo, and my grandma on my mom's side, who lives nearby. My mom is the person I talk to the most, usually in the kitchen or in the car. My dad is quieter, but he shows love by fixing things, picking people up, and worrying about bills. Mateo is thirteen and annoying in the normal little brother way, but he also asks me to draw characters for him. My grandma is important because she carries a lot of the family stories and traditions. She is the one who remembers recipes and who goes on the Día de los Muertos altar. Family is supportive, but there is pressure too, because everyone wants me to do something stable.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your grandmother?
follow_ups.response: At least once a week, sometimes more. She comes over for dinner or we go to her apartment after church or errands.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your brother do together?
follow_ups.response: We watch shows, I help him with school posters, and sometimes he comes with me when I photograph murals.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have cousins around El Paso and some family across the border, but my immediate household is my parents and brother. I am close with one cousin, Lety, who is almost like an older sister.

follow_ups.question: How often do you talk to Lety?
follow_ups.response: A few times a week by text, and we meet for coffee maybe twice a month.

follow_ups.question: What do you go to her for?
follow_ups.response: Advice about school, clothes, and when I am overthinking.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friends are Alina and Jess. Alina is into photography, and we hike or go look for murals together on weekends. Jess likes graphic novels and is the person I send weird art references to at midnight. I am also friendly with people from the library art program and a local photography club. I am not dating anyone right now. My social life is not huge, but the people I keep around understand that I can be quiet and then suddenly talk for twenty minutes about color palettes.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually spend time with friends?
follow_ups.response: Coffee shops, the library, downtown art events, or the Franklin Mountains if it is not too hot.

follow_ups.question: Do you prefer big groups or one-on-one?
follow_ups.response: One-on-one or small groups. Big parties drain me unless there is music or art to focus on.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live on the east side of El Paso, in the 79938 area. It is spread out, lots of newer houses, desert lots, shopping centers, and families driving everywhere. You can see the mountains in the distance, which I love, but you also feel how car-dependent it is. There are food trucks, taquerias, chain stores, schools, and parks, but not always sidewalks that feel nice for walking. It feels very bilingual and family-oriented. A lot of people are working hard, commuting, taking kids to school, and doing errands after work.

follow_ups.question: What places do you go to most near home?
follow_ups.response: The grocery store, a nearby park, coffee places, and the busier shopping centers when my mom needs errands.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel connected to neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A little. We say hi, but we are closer to family and friends than the whole block.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: Mostly safe, especially during the day. At night I am more careful because some streets are empty and poorly lit, so I do not walk alone late.

follow_ups.question: What makes you feel safe?
follow_ups.response: Families around, familiar streets, and my parents knowing the area.

follow_ups.question: What makes you cautious?
follow_ups.response: Loose dogs, dark sidewalks, and random cars slowing down.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The good part is family, culture, food, and the desert light. The hard part is distance: to get to downtown art events or the library program, I need rides, gas money, or careful planning.

follow_ups.question: Would you stay in El Paso long term?
follow_ups.response: Probably yes as a home base, but I want to travel for residencies.

follow_ups.question: What would improve the area?
follow_ups.response: Better buses, safer walking paths, and more youth art spaces on this side of town.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is me, my mom Maribel, my dad Rogelio, and my brother Mateo. My parents share the main expenses. My brother is in middle school. I have my room, but it also becomes an art storage room because I keep canvases, markers, and thrifted frames there. My grandma does not live with us, but she comes over often.

follow_ups.question: What is the household rhythm like in the morning?
follow_ups.response: My dad leaves early, my mom gets Mateo moving, and I usually make coffee after the first wave of noise.

follow_ups.question: Where do you make art at home?
follow_ups.response: Mostly my bedroom desk, sometimes the kitchen table if I need more space.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone living here is permanent.

follow_ups.question: Any plans for that to change soon?
follow_ups.response: No, not soon.

follow_ups.question: Would you move out for school?
follow_ups.response: Not for community college. I would commute.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Sometimes my cousin Lety sleeps over after family gatherings, but not often.

follow_ups.question: How often is that?
follow_ups.response: Maybe every couple of months.

follow_ups.question: Anyone else?
follow_ups.response: No, mostly just visitors for dinner.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everyone who lives here is here.

follow_ups.question: No one away for school?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: No one hospitalized?
follow_ups.response: No, thankfully.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My week depends on family errands, art deadlines I set for myself, and volunteer days. On normal weekdays I wake around 8:30 or 9, make coffee, help clean, sketch or work on Illustrator files, and help my brother after school if my mom is busy. Two afternoons a week I try to go to the library youth art program or help prepare materials. Weekends are more social: hiking with the photography club if the weather is okay, watching El Paso Locomotive FC on TV, or family meals. I journal at night and usually sketch while listening to Tycho or norteño music.

follow_ups.question: What is your most productive time of day?
follow_ups.response: Late morning for planning, late night for creative bursts.

follow_ups.question: What throws off your routine?
follow_ups.response: Family errands, heat, and me scrolling too long before starting.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I am not in the paid workforce right now. I do unpaid volunteer work with youth art programming and occasional community mural projects. It is usually afternoons or weekends, not a formal schedule. I have done small informal design favors, like flyers for family events, but not steady paid work. My main focus is getting ready for school and building a portfolio.

follow_ups.question: Are you looking for paid work?
follow_ups.response: I am open to part-time work if it fits school and art, maybe at a library, museum, print shop, or coffee shop.

follow_ups.question: Do you consider your art work even when unpaid?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because it takes planning, communication, and real hours, even if it is not income yet.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help around the house: dishes, laundry, sometimes cooking dinner if my mom works late, and watching my brother after school. I also help translate or explain online forms to my parents sometimes, because I am comfortable going back and forth in English and Spanish. I keep track of my own art deadlines in a planner, though I do not always follow it perfectly.

follow_ups.question: What do you cook most often?
follow_ups.response: Rice, beans, eggs, tacos, and when I am in a creative mood, chiles rellenos with quinoa filling.

follow_ups.question: What forms do you help with?
follow_ups.response: School messages, health portal stuff, bills, or anything with too much official English.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Since graduating, my schedule became less structured. At first that felt nice, then it got stressful because nobody was telling me what to do every hour. I started using a weekly planner and setting library volunteer days so I would not just drift. I also added yoga once in a while downtown, mostly for stress and stretching after sitting at my desk.

follow_ups.question: What has been hardest about the change?
follow_ups.response: Feeling like I have to prove I am not wasting time.

follow_ups.question: What has improved?
follow_ups.response: I have more time to make art that actually feels like mine.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children. The kid routine I know is my brother's: school during the day, homework after, and sometimes soccer or gaming with friends.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with his routine?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I remind him about homework or help with projects.

follow_ups.question: Do you expect to have children soon?
follow_ups.response: No, not anytime soon.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have not had a serious personal experience with law enforcement. Mostly traffic stops in the family or seeing police at school events. In El Paso, you are aware of Border Patrol too, even if you are a citizen, because it is part of the environment. I have not been arrested or anything like that, but I do feel nervous around police sometimes, especially when relatives are driving and everyone gets quiet.

follow_ups.question: Why do you think everyone gets quiet?
follow_ups.response: Because even a simple stop can feel tense when you are Mexican-American and used to being questioned.

follow_ups.question: Have police ever come to your home?
follow_ups.response: No, not for us.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: A Border Patrol checkpoint on a family trip stands out. Nothing happened, but I remember my parents being very careful and formal.

follow_ups.question: How old were you?
follow_ups.response: Maybe twelve or thirteen.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect how you see authority?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it made authority feel uneven, like some people move through it easier than others.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: No one in my immediate family has been arrested. I know of a distant cousin who had trouble years ago, but it is not part of my daily life.

follow_ups.question: Has that shaped family conversations?
follow_ups.response: Mostly as warnings about being careful who you ride with or hang around.

follow_ups.question: Any close friends arrested?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I voted in 2024 because I had just turned eighteen, and it felt important. I do not know if I will be a person who votes in every single tiny election, but I want to be consistent. My parents talk about politics, but sometimes they are tired of it. For me, voting felt like one way to have a voice, especially as a young Mexican-American woman in Texas.

follow_ups.question: How did you learn what was on the ballot?
follow_ups.response: I used voter guides, talked to my teacher, and looked things up online.

follow_ups.question: Did your friends vote?
follow_ups.response: Some did, some did not. A few were intimidated by the process.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would say I lean Democratic, but I am still forming my views. I care about immigration, education, health care, reproductive rights, LGBTQ people being treated with respect, and funding for arts and libraries. I also care about workers because my parents work hard and still have to watch every bill. At the same time, I grew up around people who are religious, family-focused, and practical, so I do not like when politics talks down to them. I am skeptical of politicians in general, but I trust local community organizers, teachers, librarians, and people who actually show up. I am not super ideological in the way older people argue online. I mostly ask: does this help families, students, and communities like mine live with dignity?

follow_ups.question: What issue feels most personal?
follow_ups.response: Education and immigration. Even when my own paperwork is simple, the stress around belonging is part of my family's story.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss politics at home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but carefully. My dad gets frustrated with both parties, and my mom cares more about practical costs.

follow_ups.question: Where do arts fit into politics for you?
follow_ups.response: Murals, libraries, and youth programs are civic life. They keep people connected and proud.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more aware of local politics. Before, I mostly thought about presidents and big national issues. Volunteering at the library made me notice how city budgets and school decisions affect real programs. I also became more serious about voting after 2024 because the process stopped feeling abstract. My views moved from just 'I care about fairness' to asking who funds services and who gets ignored.

follow_ups.question: What made local politics visible?
follow_ups.response: Seeing programs depend on staff, space, supplies, and whether anyone thinks art for kids matters.

follow_ups.question: Has any view become less certain?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I am less quick to judge people for not voting because now I see how confusing and exhausting it can be.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: It affected me somewhat to a lot. I am not Black, so I try not to act like I know that experience, but it made me think about policing, racism, and whose fear gets believed. In El Paso, race and ethnicity are also tied to language, immigration, and the border. The conversations made me pay attention to how different communities can support each other without pretending our experiences are identical.

follow_ups.question: Where did you first follow those conversations?
follow_ups.response: Instagram, school discussions, and a few documentaries or videos teachers shared.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect your art?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I became more careful about symbolism and about not using other people's pain as decoration.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the issues are about accountability and whose lives are treated as valuable. It made me think about police budgets, school security, and how quickly people label young people as dangerous. I also think movements get simplified online, and then families argue about slogans instead of the actual problems. I try to listen first, especially to Black creators, writers, and local voices.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about it with family?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. It can get tense, so I usually bring up specific stories instead of starting with slogans.

follow_ups.question: What do you wish people understood?
follow_ups.response: That asking for accountability is not the same as hating every individual officer.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race in the U.S. is everywhere, even when people say it is not. For me, being Mexican-American in El Paso means I am in a majority-Latino place, but I still know the country sees us in certain ways. Language matters too; speaking Spanish can feel normal in one room and judged in another. I have been thinking a lot about how art can show mixed identity without making it cute or simple.

follow_ups.question: When do you feel most aware of race or ethnicity?
follow_ups.response: When traveling outside El Paso, filling forms, or hearing people talk about immigrants like they are all one thing.

follow_ups.question: Does being bilingual shape that?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. Switching languages feels like home, but it also reminds me who is allowed to be comfortable.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I mostly talked with friends and shared resources online. I did not join big protests, partly because of family concerns and transportation, but I paid attention and had conversations.

follow_ups.question: What did you share online?
follow_ups.response: Art, reading lists, donation links, and posts from people directly affected.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever disagree with friends?
follow_ups.response: A little, mostly about whether posting is enough. I think it cannot be the only thing.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My friends are generally supportive of racial justice conversations. My parents are sympathetic but cautious; they worry about protests becoming unsafe and about people losing jobs or getting targeted. My brother mostly learns from what he sees online and asks questions. In my family, conversations usually connect back to immigration and being treated with respect.

follow_ups.question: Who is most vocal?
follow_ups.response: My friend Jess is the most vocal online.

follow_ups.question: Who is most cautious?
follow_ups.response: My dad. He agrees with fairness but does not trust big public conflict.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I am healthy. I do not have a major medical condition. I get headaches sometimes when I skip water or stare at screens too long, and I get anxious when deadlines pile up. I try to hike, do occasional yoga, and eat decent food at home, but I also drink too much coffee and stay up late drawing.

follow_ups.question: How often do you exercise?
follow_ups.response: Maybe two or three times a week if you count hikes, walking, yoga, or track drills.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a regular doctor?
follow_ups.response: Not really my own regular doctor. We use clinics when needed.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easier because my family cooks at home a lot, and I like hiking. It is harder because of transportation, money, heat, and screen time. If it is 100 degrees, I am not hiking. Also stress makes me snack or drink coffee instead of eating an actual meal.

follow_ups.question: What healthy meal do you like?
follow_ups.response: Fish tacos with tamarind glaze and cabbage, or pozole with extra vegetables.

follow_ups.question: What habit would you change?
follow_ups.response: Sleeping earlier. That would fix a lot.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing big like a broken bone or diagnosis. The main thing was stress during my last year of high school and after graduation. I had stomachaches and headaches when I was overwhelmed, but they improved when I started journaling and making a schedule. I also had a bad ankle twist on a hike, but it healed with rest.

follow_ups.question: Did you get medical care for the ankle?
follow_ups.response: No, we iced it and wrapped it. If it had gotten worse, we would have gone in.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone suggest counseling?
follow_ups.response: A school counselor mentioned it, but I did not start regular therapy.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not stopped me from working or helping at home. Stress slows me down sometimes, but it has not made me unable to function.

follow_ups.question: What does stress slowing you down look like?
follow_ups.response: Avoiding emails, staying in bed longer, or revising art too much.

follow_ups.question: How do you get moving again?
follow_ups.response: A list, coffee, music, and sometimes texting Alina for accountability.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: My grandma has diabetes and some blood pressure issues, so that is something we pay attention to. My mom reminds her about food and appointments. It affects the family because someone needs to drive her, translate sometimes, or help with pharmacy things. It is not an emergency all the time, but it is always in the background.

follow_ups.question: Do you help directly?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I help read instructions or go along to appointments if my mom cannot.

follow_ups.question: Has it changed family meals?
follow_ups.response: A little. We try to make lighter versions, but Mexican family food is still Mexican family food.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: It is manageable but stressful. Appointments can take time, insurance details are confusing, and costs make everyone pause before going. I have delayed care for minor things, like headaches or ankle pain, because we figured it would pass. My family tries not to go unless it feels necessary, which is common around us.

follow_ups.question: What is the biggest barrier?
follow_ups.response: Cost and knowing what insurance will actually cover.

follow_ups.question: Who handles appointments?
follow_ups.response: Mostly my mom, but I help with online portals or English paperwork.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Yes, informal remedies are normal in my family. Teas for stomachaches, vapor rub, caldo when you are sick, aloe for skin, and my grandma has strong opinions about herbal remedies. We still believe in doctors, but home care comes first for small things.

follow_ups.question: Any specific remedies you use?
follow_ups.response: Manzanilla tea for stomach stress and honey-lime for a sore throat.

follow_ups.question: Do you see that as cultural?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it is family knowledge, not something we separate from everyday care.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke, and I do not really drink. I am nineteen, so drinking is not part of my normal life. During tough times I drink coffee, journal, sketch, scroll too much, or take a walk. Sometimes I stress-bake or help cook because chopping things calms me down.

follow_ups.question: Do friends drink around you?
follow_ups.response: Some do at parties, but I am not really in that scene.

follow_ups.question: What is your most common coping habit?
follow_ups.response: Sketching while listening to music.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or other substances. I take basic pain medicine like ibuprofen if I have cramps or a headache. The most recent time was probably for a headache after working too long on my laptop. I took it, drank water, and turned the screen brightness down.

follow_ups.question: Any prescription medication?
follow_ups.response: No regular prescriptions.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel pressure to use substances socially?
follow_ups.response: Not really. My friends know I am not into it.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: My parents handle most of it through whatever insurance and clinic options they have from work or local providers. We compare costs, use clinics, and avoid unnecessary visits. For my grandma, the family coordinates rides and prescriptions. It is not luxurious, but we manage by planning and not ignoring serious things.

follow_ups.question: Do health costs affect other spending?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially prescriptions or unexpected appointments.

follow_ups.question: Who worries most about it?
follow_ups.response: My mom. She tracks everything.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally pro-vaccine. I had routine vaccines and COVID shots. I understand people being nervous, but I trust vaccines more than random internet rumors.

follow_ups.question: Did your family agree?
follow_ups.response: Mostly yes, though people asked questions first.

follow_ups.question: What made you comfortable?
follow_ups.response: Doctors, school requirements, and seeing vulnerable family members.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: Doctors, pharmacists, the CDC website if I am looking something up, and sometimes school or clinic information. I also trust my mom when she has talked to a medical person directly. I do not trust TikTok for medical decisions, even if I see health content there.

follow_ups.question: Do you check Spanish-language sources?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes if I am explaining something to family.

follow_ups.question: What source do you avoid?

follow_ups.question: What did you learn from him?
follow_ups.response: Practical problem-solving and not wasting things.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for warehouse, distribution, and delivery businesses. They moved products, stocked inventory, and got orders where they needed to go. It was not glamorous, but it kept the household going.

follow_ups.question: Was it physically demanding?
follow_ups.response: Yes, very.

follow_ups.question: Did he have benefits?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes basic benefits, but not always great.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope I am in school or finishing an associate's degree in graphic design or visual communication. I want to transfer later for museum studies or cultural arts management. I hope I have paid work connected to art, maybe with a museum, nonprofit, library, or community arts program. I want to travel to Oaxaca for embroidery or textile study, and I want to keep doing murals in El Paso. I also hope I can help my parents more financially and maybe have my own small studio corner someday. I do not need a fancy life; I want a life where my art, family, culture, and work are connected.

follow_ups.question: What is the first concrete step?
follow_ups.response: Finish my portfolio and enroll at EPCC.

follow_ups.question: What would success feel like?
follow_ups.response: Getting paid to create spaces where kids and families see their stories respected.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value family, culture, creativity, and being useful to my community. I value remembering where we come from without being trapped by it. I value kindness that actually does something, not just nice words. And I value art because it lets people say complicated things when normal language is not enough.

follow_ups.question: What value did your family teach most?
follow_ups.response: Showing up for each other.

follow_ups.question: What value feels most yours?
follow_ups.response: Creative honesty, like making work that is beautiful but also true.

summaries.demographer: Zoila Pizano is a 19-year-old never-married Mexican-American/Latina woman born and living in El Paso, Texas, specifically the east side/79938 area (Q84-Q89, Q97). She has a high school diploma, graduated in 2025, is not currently enrolled in school, and is planning community college for graphic design or visual communication (Q90-Q92). She lives in a rented household with both parents, Maribel and Rogelio, and her 13-year-old brother Mateo, with no children or partner (Q05, Q11, Q51-Q58). She is not in the paid workforce and depends economically on her parents while contributing unpaid household, translation, sibling, and volunteer art labor (Q16-Q17, Q55, Q65-Q73).
summaries.behavioral_economist: Zoila shows strong future orientation but limited liquidity: she saves small amounts for school, art tools, and Oaxaca travel, while a $400 emergency would nearly wipe out her personal cushion (Q61-Q62, Q82). Her decisions balance identity investment and financial constraint, most clearly in choosing a gap year and portfolio-building over immediate full-time retail work (Q02, Q83). She responds to uncertainty with lists, planners, deadlines, and social accountability, but procrastination and comparison on social media can undermine follow-through (Q18, Q34, Q48, Q50). Household spending is cautious and adaptive, with cutbacks on eating out, clothes, coffee, comics, and art supplies during tight months (Q56-Q64, Q81).
summaries.political_scientist: Zoila is a young first-time voter who voted in 2024 and identifies as independent-leaning Democratic, closer to Democrats than Republicans but not strongly partisan (Q23, Q95-Q96). Her political priorities include immigration, education, health care, reproductive rights, LGBTQ respect, workers, arts funding, libraries, and local youth programs (Q24-Q25). She has moderate institutional skepticism toward politicians but relatively high trust in local organizers, teachers, librarians, doctors, pharmacists, and community workers (Q24, Q42). Her views on race and policing are shaped by Black Lives Matter, Mexican-American identity, bilingual border life, and awareness of Border Patrol and checkpoints (Q20-Q30).
summaries.psychologist: Zoila presents as creative, conscientious when externally structured, family-oriented, and identity-driven, with a self-concept anchored in art, Mexican-American heritage, and community usefulness (Q01, Q02, Q65, Q109). She reports anxiety-like overthinking and procrastination without a formal diagnosis, especially after losing the structure of high school (Q43-Q45). Her coping strategies are mostly adaptive: journaling, sketching, hiking, yoga, music, cooking, planning, and seeking support from her mother, cousin, and close friends (Q34, Q38, Q44-Q50). Relationally, she prefers small trusted circles, values showing up for family, and negotiates independence with guilt and gratitude while still living at home (Q05-Q07, Q83, Q109).
